content: My starter has been sluggish this week — taking 10 hours to peak instead of the usual 5-6. I haven't changed my feeding ratio or flour. Could be the temperature drop — my kitchen is running about 66°F now that fall hit.

Temperature has a huge impact on fermentation rate. At 66°F your starter's microbial activity slows significantly. You could try feeding with warmer water (85-90°F) to give it a boost, or find a warmer spot like on top of your fridge.

I actually built a proofing box with a seedling heat mat and an Inkbird temperature controller — same one I use for the fermentation chamber. Set it to 78°F and the starter should be back on schedule.
That's a solid setup. A consistent 78°F is ideal for starter activity. The Inkbird controller keeps it precise, which removes one more variable from your baking process.

Exactly — the thing is, baking and engineering have the same core principle: control your variables and the outcomes become predictable. My proofing box is basically a PID controller for fermentation.
The parallel is surprisingly strong. Both are about understanding a system well enough to control its inputs and predict its outputs.

Ha, yeah. My wife thinks I'm overthinking bread but the crumb doesn't lie. Anyway, I also want to try a rye flour addition to the starter — maybe 10% rye — since rye has more wild yeast and minerals. Should boost the fermentation activity.
